items.title: Gang Members Violently Murder Christians, Torch Church
items.author: Tré Goins-Phillips
items.summary: PRAY.
items.content:
📖 News | Faithwire

At least 47 people and 22 others were injured Sunday night into Monday morning when gang members attacked a church providing shelter to displaced peoples right outside Haiti’s capital, Port-au-Prince.

The mayor of Kenscoff, Massillon Jean, said the deadly assault began around 10:30 p.m. and described it as a “night of terror.”

Jean blamed the Viv Ansanm gang coalition, one of the largest groups of violent gang members in Haiti.

According to an official statement, the Haitian government sent reinforcements to help local area police.

“Let there be no mistake: this time of mourning is also a challenge,” said the press release. “And to this challenge, the government responds with the force of law and the legitimate exercise of state force.”

It continued, “All security forces have been placed on maximum alert. Reinforcements are being deployed. The orders are clear: protect, secure, intervene. Government authority will be restored — firmly and without delay — throughout the entire territory of Kenscoff.”

The government added “no armed group will thrive in Haiti” and “[c]riminals will find no truce, no refuge, and no impunity.”

Haitian Bishop Joseph Gontrand Décoste of Jérémie told Aid to the Church in Need (ACN) that churches and Christians as a whole are increasingly the targets of gang violence because believers remain the last stalwart resistance against wrongdoing.

“We are the last remaining bulkhead — moral, ethical, spiritual, and prophetic,” he said. “That is why they want to eliminate us.”

For context, about 40 Catholic parishes have shut down in Port-au-Prince as Christians have faced increasingly deadly violence. In the first seven months of 2026, two priests were abducted and a seminarian was murdered. Last spring, two nuns from the Little Sisters of Saint Thérèse were killed and, in 2024, nine religious sisters, five brothers, and four priests were kidnapped.

ACN has reported gangs control somewhere between 70% and 90% of the capital city of Port-au-Prince.

items.title: Where God Reigns
items.author: Marvin Williams
items.summary:
In 2018, a man checked into a room at New York hotel for a one-night stay. Remarkably, he used the room for five years without paying another cent—exploiting obscure rent laws to hold on to it. His refusal to leave, however, eventually led to potential prison time for him.
Like an unwelcome te
items.content:
📖 Devotional | Our Daily Bread

In 2018, a man checked into a room at New York hotel for a one-night stay. Remarkably, he used the room for five years without paying another cent—exploiting obscure rent laws to hold on to it. His refusal to leave, however, eventually led to potential prison time for him.

Like an unwelcome tenant who overstays, James warns us that the devil lingers in our lives when left unchecked. “Resist the devil,” James writes, “and he will flee from you” (4:7). The apostle emphasizes that our struggles often come from impure “desires” and “wrong motives” (vv. 1, 3)—things like pride, divided loyalties, and impure thoughts residing in our hearts. To counter such temptation, James offers two commands: “submit . . . to God” and “resist the devil” (v. 7). To submit means surrendering every part of our lives to God. Resisting the devil is equally active, requiring prayer, vigilance, and the wisdom of Scripture.

Like a landlord evicting an unlawful tenant, in God’s strength we can refuse to let the temptation of the devil overtake us. As we resist him, God promises victory as James asserts: “He will flee from you” (v. 7).

When we evict sin and the devil’s influence and “come near to God” (v. 8), we allow His peace, joy, and purpose to dwell more fully in us. The enemy can’t stay where God reigns!

items.author: Lisa M. Samra
items.summary:
Speaking to a group of young actors, Academy-Award-winning actor Denzel Washington encouraged them to begin each day with prayer, suggesting they “put your shoes way under the bed at night” to ensure they "gotta get on your knees in the morning.”
Developing a regular habit of praye
items.content:
📖 Devotional | Our Daily Bread

Speaking to a group of young actors, Academy-Award-winning actor Denzel Washington encouraged them to begin each day with prayer, suggesting they “put your shoes way under the bed at night” to ensure they "gotta get on your knees in the morning.”

Developing a regular habit of prayer might take some thoughtful and even creative planning, but it’s a practice that has sustained God’s people throughout history—especially in difficult times. We see this in the life of Daniel, who was served in King Darius’ administration. He quickly distinguished himself as the top government advisor, which angered local officials. Out of jealously they plotted to oust the prophet, but they quickly realized the only charge that would stick was related to Daniel’s well-known habit of prayer. Even after the officials tricked the king into making it illegal for Daniel to pray, Daniel still “got down on his knees, and prayed . . . just as he had done before” (Daniel 6:10).

A consistent prayer life was essential for Daniel to experience God’s sustaining strength and peace (Psalm 29:11). It helped him to triumph over the forces seeking to destroy him. In the same way, establishing a regular time to meet with God in prayer and making it a daily priority can help cultivate our relationship with Him. During each difficulty we face, it’s His strength that will sustain us.

items.title: ‘The Church Deserves the Best Music’: Michael Cochren’s New Album Is His Argument for It
items.author: Taylor Berry
items.summary: For a few years in his early twenties, Michael Cochren played four hours a night in the only rooms in southern Indiana that paid for live music: clubs, VFW posts, moose lodges. Covers, mostly. What he brought into those rooms was a strange pile of influences. His grandparents sang in church; an aunt
items.content:
📖 Culture | Relevant Magazine

For a few years in his early twenties, Michael Cochren played four hours a night in the only rooms in southern Indiana that paid for live music: clubs, VFW posts, moose lodges. Covers, mostly.

What he brought into those rooms was a strange pile of influences. His grandparents sang in church; an aunt played gospel piano and taught him. His grandfather loved big band. His dad played him Jackson Browne and Billy Joel, then Ray Charles. His mom had the Delilah show on in the evenings, which meant Phil Collins and Michael Bolton. He loved *NSYNC when *NSYNC came around.

“A true melting pot,” he said.

Then he got to college. His faith stopped being something he’d inherited, and his songs changed with it.

He’d been writing for girls — “I just wanted to be cool” — and started writing what he describes as journal entries instead. Hey, I’m pretty messed up, and I see that now, and God’s grace is working on me.

The bar bookings dried up.

“That’s not what they paid me to come and do,” he said. “They didn’t pay me to come have church.”

The record he put out in May, Runs in the Blood, is where the melting pot finally shows. There’s more Ray Charles in it — organ, rasp, a rhythm section that swings. He names Adele, Chris Stapleton and Teddy Swims among the people he studies now, and Benson Boone for melodies.

“Every record cycle I’m looking for a new angle, because we have the same message as a Christian artist. We’re saying the same timeless truths,” he said. “But there is an endless way that we say them and how they can sound and how they can feel.”

He says the standard is not negotiable. “I feel like the church deserves the best. The church deserves to have the best music. And so I think we have the responsibility to always be getting better.”

The album title has two meanings, and he built the record around both. One is his family: the faith his grandparents handed down. For the cover, a Nashville creative agency drove trucks and a bus up to Indiana, built a set in his 98-year-old grandmother’s woods, and hung her own knickknacks and family photographs on the walls they’d built.

The other meaning is the one he’d rather talk about. “It’s also about what runs in the blood of Jesus that has washed me, that washes all of us.”

Underneath both is the thing he says has been his subject since the beginning. “The message that permeates all of our music is hope. It is second chances,” he said. “That’s always been kind of my thing — I’ve been given this second chance. If I only had one shot, I blew that a long time ago.”

He has a specific second chance in mind. For eight years of their marriage, he and his wife tried to have a child and couldn’t.

“I felt like it was never gonna happen,” he said. The verse he kept returning to was Romans 8:28, that God works all things for the good of those who love him. “I have to rest in that constantly. Even when it doesn’t feel good, that’s when the rubber hits the road, and that’s when faith really is forged — when you have to trust that God is doing something good and it feels really bad.”

Their son was born in January. The album was already finished; Cochren was holding the baby while he approved the final masters.

“I’m holding my offspring in my arms and it’s like, wow. God, you are really blessing me here.”

The kid came to his first show recently. Partway through the set Cochren tells the audience about the eight years, and he looked out mid-story and saw him down front in a tiny pair of headphones.

He is careful about what he wants that to mean.

“I know a lot of people are going to read this and see this that they’re still waiting for a yes from God, or an answer to prayer, whatever that prayer may be,” he said. “And one thing that I always want to communicate to people is, I don’t ever want to be someone that just says that God is good because he gave me what I wanted. God was just as good to me in the eight years in the valley, in the pit. Because if he wasn’t, I wouldn’t be here. I wouldn’t have made it. I wouldn’t have survived.”

“He was so kind and good and holding me even when I was just mad and angry and it didn’t feel good at all. God was just as good to me in my longing as he was in my receiving.”

Cochren is on planes most weekends now, which is different math than it used to be. The baby is at home.

“It is a constant battle,” he said. “As I’m getting ready to get on this plane and go, and I don’t really want to go for the weekend, I wanna be home with my baby — like, what was this all about to begin with?”

The answer he keeps landing on predates the bars, the label and the records. Before he knew what making music meant, he was a kid who danced around the living room to get his family to laugh.

“It was about just the love of creating something, the love of entertaining people, making people smile,” he said. “But God has shown me how all of that is ministry now.”

items.title: Apologetics Isn’t Dead, the Sequel: The Conversion of Joe Schmid
items.author: Justin Kalan
items.summary:
Justin Kalan

An important lesson we may gather is that converts beget converts.
items.content:
📖 Catholic Teaching | Word on Fire

Justin Kalan

Four years ago, in my first piece for Evangelization & Culture Online, I discussed the then announced conversion to Catholicism of one of the most popular Christian apologists on Youtube, Cameron Bertuzzi. One of the salient features of Bertuzzi’s conversion was the role that apologetical argument played in it. In particular, Cameron was convinced of the doctrine of the papacy by the biblical typological argument connecting St. Peter with Eliakim, an Old Testament figure mentioned in Isaiah 22. It was Suan Sonna, who also happens to be a convert to Catholicism, whose exposition of this argument helped bring Bertuzzi to Catholicism.

It was a joyous surprise the other day when I found out that Joe Schmid, an agnostic PhD student in philosophy at Princeton and longtime YouTuber, had also converted to Catholicism. 

In one way, Schmid’s conversion is more striking than Bertuzzi’s because he is not merely coming to Catholicism from another Christian denomination but from agnosticism. Though raised Catholic, for years, Schmid has run a very interesting YouTube channel called Majesty of Reason, which focuses on various topics in philosophy, taking particular interest in arguments for and against God’s existence. Indeed, a number of his videos are of him debunking arguments for God’s existence and making arguments against theism and Christianity. 

Schmid outlined his journey from his Catholic upbringing into atheism, agnosticism, and then finally back to the Catholic faith in a video on his channel, and he’ll be appearing on other channels to discuss his conversion as well. Schmid and Bertuzzi both run in some of the same apologetics circles online, and their conversions bear some notable similarities.

Schmid’s Conversion to Theism

Schmid’s conversion followed a logical order, starting with an increasing confidence in God’s existence and then moving towards more specific beliefs in Christianity and finally Catholicism in particular. Schmid notes that during the first few years of his PhD studies, many of his objections to God’s existence, including things like the problem of evil, began to be answered, and many of his previous objections to God’s existence began to fade away. 

For instance, Schmid was impressed by the argument of fine-tuning the universe for life and, more generally, of theism’s broad explanatory power as a simple hypothesis to explain the universe, beauty, our moral intuitions, and many other things. Like Bertuzzi, Schmid was also struck by the immense beauty in the created world that pointed him toward God.

Miracles and the Case for Catholicism

Convinced of theism, Schmid was faced with a variety of evidence for Catholicism during this early period in his PhD program that has played an undersized role in Catholic apologetics in recent years: Catholic miracles. From Eucharistic miracles, to Padre Pio, to Marian apparitions, Schmid was struck by the overwhelming evidence these miracles claim and support, as well as their implications regarding the Catholic faith. 

Schmid’s conversion seems to support a claim Bertuzzi made during a recent Catholic apologetics conference hosted by Trent Horn that miracles are an undertapped source of evidence for Catholicism and should be investigated and shared further. Bertuzzi’s comment has proved prophetic. Just a few weeks ago, Ethan Muse, an up-and-coming Catholic apologist himself and fellow graduate student in philosophy, was on Matt Fradd’s podcast for five hours discussing Catholic miracles, making waves in apologetics circles.

According to Schmid, it was the very same Ethan Muse who routinely took the time to converse with him and share with him the extraordinary evidence for certain Catholic miracles as well as respond to Schmid’s various objections to the Catholic faith toward the end of Schmid’s journey to conversion.

Beyond Argument: The Role of the Saints and Conscience

No conversion consists of an intellectual change alone. Rather, metanoia, or conversion, is a change of the whole person that goes beyond (meta) the mind (nous). A couple of details from Schmid’s account of his conversion reaffirm this truth.
Word on Fire’s Liturgy of the Hours is Here!
Order Your Set Today

First, Schmid notes that the powerful story of St. Maria Goretti caused him to seek after the same strong desire for purity and love that she showed in her short life. At the same time, Schmid notes that his conscience began to convict him more and more of his own personal sin and how short he was falling from the life God calls us to. Thus evidence, inspiration from saints, internal witness of conscience, and other religious experiences were all part of what Schmid describes as a “frontal assault” by God against Schmid’s non-belief, which culminated in him going to confession for the first time in many years several months ago and coming back into communion with the Church.

The Upshot

There are a couple lessons that both Bertuzzi and now Schmid’s conversions teach us. First, no one’s conversion (or reversion) to Catholicism is due entirely to apologetic arguments. People are not mere intellects but body and soul creatures with a deep spiritual, emotional, and rational life. As Schmid himself testifies, what drew him back to the Catholic faith was a variety of experiences that God providentially ordered. However, as a philosopher, reason and argument played an indispensable role in Schmid’s conversion just as it did in Bertuzzi’s a few years ago. 

Arguments for God’s existence should be investigated, refined, and utilized in apologetics. This is why Bishop Barron in his introductory lecture at the launch of The New Ressourcement journal noted, “Theologians of a new ressourcement should enter into renewed dialogue with Aquinas precisely on this point of demonstrating God’s existence.” Moreover, arguments for Catholicism, specifically Catholic miracles, can and should be used to demonstrate the truth of the Catholic faith. 

Another lesson we may gather is that converts beget converts. Bertuzzi was deeply impacted by Suan Sonna’s case for Catholicism. Sonna himself was brought into the faith by some of his college friends, some who were themselves converts to Catholicism. Ethan Muse is a recent convert, and he seems to have played a vital role in Schmid’s reversion to Catholicism. This Pauline zeal for the faith demonstrated in these converts helps to power their important ministry in reaching out to nonbelievers who in turn can reach out to others and so forth. The role of one single person can make a remarkable difference not just in another’s life, but indirectly in the lives of all those shaped by that other person too.

What’s Next?

Schmid’s channel’s focus will no longer be philosophy in general but on the case for God’s existence and Catholicism. With Schmid’s intellect and his already impressive résumé, we can expect some great material from him in the future. 

Despite having met Schmid briefly only once and having had only one or two interactions with him online, I cannot overstate how thrilled I am by this news and will continue praying for him on his journey with Christ.

items.title: Dolly Parton’s Christian Witness
items.author: Dr. Kody W. Cooper
items.summary:
Dr. Kody W. Cooper

It seems Dolly was one of the few remaining persons in American life who was widely beloved and respected across political and cultural divides.
items.content:
📖 Catholic Teaching | Word on Fire

Dr. Kody W. Cooper

As I was lecturing earlier this week to a classroom of mostly native Tennesseans, a couple of students suddenly burst aloud: “Dolly Parton is dead!” I was explaining the concept of the “common good” and identifying possible common goods that people share across left and right (in a class pretty evenly split between left and right). My no-electronic-device-policy was apparently no match for the burst of 911 texts and alerts the students were receiving. The class was obviously stunned and, despite priding myself on being able to seamlessly integrate just about any comment or question into a lecture, I found myself at a loss for how to return to the topic at hand. Then one student chimed in: “We can all agree that Dolly Parton was a common good!” 

Indeed, judging by the accolades from across the political spectrum, it seems Dolly was one of the few remaining persons in American life who was widely beloved and respected across political and cultural divides. Dolly was something of a goddess in Tennessee. Yet, I confess, it took me a while to grasp the reasons for her cult of personality. 

My earliest memory of Dolly Parton is not like that of generations older than Millennials. I wasn’t alive during her early years performing in Knoxville and Nashville. Nor during her national rise to stardom in the ’70s with hits like “Jolene” and “I Will Always Love You.” (Indeed, as a ’90s kid, my earliest memory of the latter song was the rendition by Whitney Houston.) And unlike middle-aged and younger Southerners, I didn’t grow up going to Dollywood in Pigeon Forge, Tennessee. As a Midwesterner, my earliest recollection of the Dolly phenomenon is probably a family trip I took as a kid to the spinoff Dixie Stampede in Branson, Missouri. While the show has evolved over the years (it has since been rebranded Dolly Parton’s Stampede), its essence remains: a patriotic, family-friendly dinner variety show of singing, dancing, horseback riding, rings of fire, and the age-old conflict of North versus South. I still remember drinking from my little slice of Americana: a novelty Dixie Stampede cowboy boot cup.

But it wasn’t until I moved to Tennessee that I learned more about Dolly’s life. As charmingly recounted in A Coat of Many Colors, a television movie with just the right amount of schmaltz, she grew up poor in the Smoky Mountains in a one-room cabin, one of twelve children, who slept several to a bed, with a loving mother and father whose Christian faith was central to their lives and upbringing. It was her mother’s deep Christian faith, Dolly recounts, that was the beating heart of their home. In one scene, the clan of Parton children descend upon their parents’ bed in their PJs, and Mama Parton breaks into song: “We got no money. but we’re rich in love . . .” The idea of the movie—encapsulated in the original song of the same name—is that happiness in this world consists not in mammon but the bonds of familial love in a Christian home. 

Something of a biopic of her early childhood that Dolly herself produced and narrated, A Coat of Many Colors (which originally aired on NBC) stands out as an extraordinarily unlikely pro-marriage, pro-life, and pro-natal network telecast. It positively portrays rural, big family life in 1950s Tennessee, advocates a Christian vision of faith and forgiveness, and holds out hope for eternal life for children who die before childbirth, including her little brother, Larry.

From her humble beginnings, Dolly rose to become a successful artist, businesswoman, and capitalist, with an estimated worth in the hundreds of millions of dollars. Unlike many artists, she retained the publishing rights to her songs and reaped the attendant royalties. And her theme parks have only grown in popularity and success, with Dollywood recently surpassing Disney World as Americans’ favorite theme park. America’s favorite theme park includes the Robert F. Thomas chapel, where you can hear gospel music any day of the week and catch a nondenominational service on Sundays.

Dolly showed that it is possible to remain rich in love despite being wealthy. She was a philanthropist, noted for her passion for causes like education, in light of her father’s illiteracy. She believed, in tune with the traditional Christian teaching of the ordo amoris, that charity begins at home, leading efforts to fundraise and help people rebuild their lives after the catastrophic Smoky Mountains wildfires of 2016. And her idea to provide books for children in Sevier County, Tennessee, to combat illiteracy grew into the Imagination Library, which gives a free book every month to children from birth to age five not only in Tennessee but several partner states and counties across the US, and even internationally in Canada, the UK, Ireland, and Australia.  

Despite her wealth and the apparent ability to hire a chef or eat out for all meals, Dolly embraced one the most mundane and yet profound acts of love that animates a Christian home and animated her as a devoted wife, sister, aunt, and friend: cooking. “God, family, music, and food are the staples of my life,” she wrote. She joyfully embraced making mouth-watering Southern breakfasts for her husband Carl, to whom she was married for fifty-nine years. 

Indeed, the theme of hunger for food and the friendship that accompanies a blessed meal as the occasion of seeking and finding spiritual nourishment underlies the biblical story of Joseph that Dolly’s movie and song allude to. And, like the bully who Dolly invites to dinner and church, it is hunger that initially motivates the prodigal son’s return to the father, perhaps the most profound parable encapsulating the Gospel message.

The sequel to A Coat of Many Colors portrays another true story from Dolly’s childhood. When Dolly’s family was snowed in by a blizzard and trapped inside their Tennessee mountain home without food, water, or firewood, they prayed for God to save them. Dolly narrates her belief that God answered that prayer by sending a guardian angel. Clearly the Lord had other plans for her. She went to her eternal reward on Tuesday, August 25, 2026.
